source.title: Meta-Task Prompting Elicits Embeddings from Large Language Models
source.authors: Yibin Lei; Di Wu; Tianyi Zhou; Tao Shen; Yu Cao; Chongyang Tao; Andrew Yates

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares sentence-embedding evaluation scores across language-model sizes, a different measure and task from pretraining-loss scaling, and reports what happens to performance as size changes.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit scaling laws, or test extrapolation. Table 7 reports an STS score sweep over three model sizes; this bears on V6. Table 8 reports transfer-task results but does not provide a model-size sweep. Other comparisons of embedding methods and prompt configurations do not test the listed scaling versions.
record.test_reason: Section 5.6 deliberately varies LLAMA2 size (7B/13B/70B) and reports downstream STS scores for training-free prompted sentence embeddings. That is a new setting with a result on whether downstream performance improves with scale (V6). It is a three-point sweep with no fit, so the evidence is thin. It is closer to T3 than T2, because no scaling-law method is applied.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that final-layer embeddings do not improve with model size, while their proportional layer selection gives the best result at 70B. They speculate this 'could point to a potential scaling law' in which larger models need a non-final layer. The claim is speculative, rests on three sizes, and is about layer choice rather than a fitted power law.
record.recipe_differences: This is a prompted sentence-embedding evaluation, not a pretraining-loss scaling-law measurement. Models are evaluated at 4-bit precision, and the output layer is selected proportionally to model depth.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported size-sweep result depends on output-layer choice: the final layer shows no size-related improvement, while a proportional layer selection gives the highest score at 70B.
record.problems: The scaling sweep covers only three LLAMA2 sizes and reports STS embedding scores rather than held-out pretraining loss. The proportional-layer comparison changes the selected layer across sizes, and Table 7 gives no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted. Table 8's transfer-task accuracies are not a model-size sweep; Figure 4 varies output layers but does not test size scaling.

untested.parts: All: no shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
All: no other modality or training regime scaling law.
Relationship between pretraining loss and downstream score; any fitted or predictive law; sizes beyond three points; transfer-task size sweep.
All: no exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: LLAMA2 7B vs 13B STS Avg. at full precision, final layer. MetaEOL scores 75.96 vs 75.56 and PromptEOL 70.03 vs 68.83, so the larger model is lower for both. Echo is 66.05 vs 72.33, so the larger model is higher. This is further size evidence that differs by method.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3 (new setting, no scaling-law methodology). The single limits_scope label was split: the final-layer rows show an absent effect, which is a challenge, while the proportional-layer rows are limits_scope. All Table 7 runs are 4-bit quantized. Prior work (Jiang et al. 2023b) also reported no STS gain with size; that result is only cited and is not a row. The study is not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law fit and several-orders-of-magnitude range.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation comparison or parameter/token allocation trend.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count using loss.
No test of power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
No pretraining-loss-to-downstream-performance analysis or fitted predictive relationship. Transfer-task accuracy is reported for one model size, while the size sweep is on STS scores for MetaEOL.
No analysis of scaling-law exponents, compute-optimal allocation fits, or their dependence on fitting choices.
